w:r.w:t: We should evolve PackProof into a unified, API-first evidence platform organized around a canonical
Commerce Context → Passport → Evidence Session → Evidence Result
The PayPal-button analogy is useful for integration simplicity, but PackProof should not imitate PayPal’s payment semantics. The PackProof button should behave like this:
The merchant installs a PackProof app, plugin, extension, or JavaScript component.
The integration supplies structured listing, product, variant, cart, or order data to PackProof.
PackProof creates an immutable, provenance-bearing commerce-context snapshot.
The button receives only a short-lived handoff token—never the merchant’s private API credential.
Clicking the button opens a hosted or native PackProof flow.
The passport form is already populated with the item description, identifiers, selected variant, price, currency, product URL, and other available information.
The user reviews and confirms the imported information instead of retyping it.
Once an actual order exists, the merchant’s server binds the passport to the authoritative order and line item.
PackProof capture, evidence, return, notification, reporting, and webhook components all operate on that same canonical record.

PackProof elements should interoperate through shared domain services, stable resource contracts, and versioned events—not by allowing every component to call every other component or write directly to Firestore.
That gives us seamless interoperability without creating an unmaintainable web of dependencies.
The existing master plan already calls for shared domain services, a stable API, webhooks, SDKs, and commerce integrations. The important sequencing change is that the
commerce-context model must be established near the beginning

, while Shopify/WooCommerce-specific adapters remain later. The current plan waits until Phase 10 to address commerce, which is too late to influence the underlying transaction model cleanly. The imported product/listing information should not be inserted directly into the transaction as an undifferentiated description. It needs a first-class provenance model.
A commerce context represents a snapshot of what the commerce system asserted about an item at a particular time.
Every imported field should retain where it came from:
Those are meaningfully different assertions and must never be collapsed into one ambiguous description.
When users review imported information, PackProof should not mutate the original listing snapshot.
For example, if a merchant listing says:
“2024 Limited Edition Watch, stainless steel, blue dial.”
“Includes original box but no warranty card.”
Which participants confirmed the resulting terms.
That is much stronger than copying text into one mutable description field.
